facts.text: It is the smallest owl on the Australian mainland, measuring 27 to 36 cm long.
facts.quote: The smallest owl on the Australian mainland, the Australian boobook is 27 to 36 cm (10.5 to 14 in) long.

facts.text: Its eyes have been described as grey-green, green-yellow, or even light hazel.
facts.quote: The eyes have been described as grey-green, green-yellow, or even light hazel.

facts.text: It hunts by pouncing on prey from a perch such as a fence, branch, or telegraph pole, then retreats to a tree to eat it.
facts.quote: Using a fence, branch, or telegraph pole as a perch or vantage point from which to hunt, the Australian boobook pounces on prey then retreats to a tree or elevated place to eat it.

facts.text: It often hunts near street- or house-lights where flying insects gather, making it a familiar presence in suburban backyards.
facts.quote: It often hunts in open areas near trees, and also where prey is likely to congregate, such as mice near haystacks or barns, or flying insects near street- or house-lights.

facts.text: The female alone incubates the eggs and is fed by the male, taking a brief dusk break of around half an hour, sometimes to bathe.
facts.quote: The female alone incubates the eggs, during which time she is fed by the male. She does leave the nest at dusk for around half an hour, sometimes to bathe.

facts.text: It is assessed as being of least concern thanks to its large range and apparently stable population.
facts.quote: The International Union for Conservation of Nature has assessed the Australian boobook as being of least concern on account of its large range and apparently stable population.

facts.text: Its two-note boo-book call can carry up to 1 km away, with the second note generally lower in pitch than the first.
facts.quote: The characteristic two-note boo-book call or hoot can be heard up to 1 km (0.6 mi) away, the second note generally lower in pitch than the first.

facts.text: The male hoots more often than the female, using his call to advertise his territory and when bringing food to his mate.
facts.quote: The male's hooting is higher pitched and of shorter duration, and is heard much more commonly than that of the female. He uses it as a contact call and to advertise his territory to females, as well as when bringing food to his mate or even before mating.

facts.text: It roosts by day in densely foliated spots in trees, often keeping several roosting sites, and may use caves or ledges if no trees are suitable.
facts.quote: It retires to densely foliated spots in trees in the daytime, each individual often having several roosting sites. Caves or ledges are alternative roosting sites if no suitable trees are available.
